criteria.note: The single most-searched-for artefact — the phrase itself, in Hangul with translation — appears inside the first 100 words, before any preamble.

Title is 52 chars including the appended ' | Gluten-Free Korea', keyword sits at the front, description is ~136 chars and adds the angle (allergy framing, copy-and-show, first answer is wrong) rather than restating the title.

Headings carry the argument rather than label it ("Why 'allergy' beats 'gluten-free' in Korea", "Reconfirming — the part people skip", "What these phrases can't do"); a skim of headings alone yields the thesis and its limits.

Five internal links, each placed where the reader's next question actually arises: /places after the geography claim, hidden-gluten after the condiment section, reading-korean-food-labels after the barley/rye gap, and the travel guide at the close.

All five Q/As are established in the body — the 글루텐프리 framing, the memorise-one-line phrase, the no-pronunciation policy, the 알러지/알레르기 spelling point, and the coeliac limits — and each stands alone as a rich result.

Real first-hand texture (the 10% wheat bakery, the year of asking, the couple-with-one-GF-person framing) but almost nothing a reader could pin to a place, a date, or an outcome, and no account of anything that went wrong.
criteria.evidence_quote: We did not count conversations or record outcomes, so this is a consistent impression, not a measured rate.

criteria.note: Precise throughout — 양조간장 vs 조선간장/한식간장 vs 혼합간장 distinguished by production method, a named product (Sempio 501), the exact allergen-label wording 알레르기 유발물질, and the 밀가루-vs-밀 distinction that most competing guides miss.

Two primary sources — a manufacturer's own product page and the statutory 시행규칙 별표 2 on law.go.kr — both linked directly and both carrying a currency stamp ("retrieved August 2026", "text in force as of August 2026").
States plainly what the method cannot establish, separates the household's NCGS reality from coeliac requirements, offers an independent verification path, and carries no commercial links at all.

findings.quote: during our first year back in Korea (2025–26), one bakery owner told us — cheerfully, without being pressed — that his was 10% wheat.
findings.why: This is the single strongest first-hand moment in the piece and it is stripped of every checkable particular: no shop name, no neighbourhood, no month. The surrounding experience claims are similarly unanchored ("across a year of asking", "between 2025 and 2026"). A reader cannot distinguish this from a plausible composite, which is exactly the signal Google's experience criterion is looking for.
findings.fix: Name the bakery and district and give a month (e.g. "a 쌀빵 bakery in Cheonan, March 2026"). Add one failure story with a consequence — a time the phrases produced a confident 'no wheat' that turned out wrong, what the dish was, and what happened next. That single paragraph would move this from 2 to 3.

findings.quote: Two habits that came out of doing this badly first:
findings.why: The sentence promises a lived mistake and then delivers only the corrected rule. The 'doing this badly' is the part with experiential value and it is skipped.
findings.fix: Spend two sentences on what going in with 글루텐프리 in a translation app actually produced — the restaurant type, the answer you got, what you ended up eating or not eating.

findings.quote: Staff who wave off 'gluten' go and ask the kitchen once they see 알러지.
findings.why: In the body this pattern is explicitly downgraded to an unmeasured impression ("We did not count conversations or record outcomes, so this is a consistent impression, not a measured rate"). Lifted into a rich result, the FAQ sentence reads as a general rule with no hedge attached, and a rich result shows without the surrounding caveat.
findings.fix: Carry the hedge into the answer itself: "In our experience, staff who wave off 'gluten' will go and ask the kitchen once they see 알러지 — an impression from a year of asking, not a measured rate."

findings.quote: **Don't try to pronounce it.** You'll notice there is no pronunciation guide anywhere in this post, and that's deliberate
findings.why: The show-don't-pronounce policy is well argued for the on-page experience, where a copy button exists. It does not survive syndication: in a Google FAQ rich result or an AI answer, the Korean string appears with no copy button and no romanisation, so a reader who arrives via that surface gets a phrase they can neither say nor easily copy.
findings.fix: Keep the body policy as is, but consider a one-line note in the FAQ answers pointing to the on-page copy buttons ("copy buttons for each line are on the guide page"), so the off-page version of the answer is still actionable.

findings.quote: (소비자 안전을 위한 표시사항, under 제5조제1항 — text in force as of August 2026)
findings.why: "In force as of" tells the reader when you checked, not when the provision was last amended. For a legal citation that a coeliac reader may act on, the amendment date is the more useful stamp and law.go.kr exposes it.
findings.fix: Add the 시행일 (effective date) of the 별표 alongside the retrieval note, e.g. "시행 2026-01-01 기준".

criteria.note: Nearly every claim is either linked to a primary source (Sempio product page, 시행규칙 별표 2) or explicitly flagged as the authors' own uncounted impression, but the traditional-soy-sauce composition claim is asserted as general fact with no source.
criteria.evidence_quote: Traditional **조선간장 / 한식간장** — the meju-based kind used for soups and namul — carries no wheat

criteria.note: No invented products, statistics, or dates — the Sempio citation, retrieval date, and regulation reference are all checkable and mutually consistent — but the stated geographic scope of the authors' experience shifts between two passages.
criteria.evidence_quote: We are describing what has worked for us in Seoul and Gyeonggi as a couple managing NCGS.

criteria.note: The piece states plainly that its basis is uncounted first-hand experience and a shopping habit, and names what that cannot establish — no sample, no measurement, no lab test — without dressing any of it up as analysis.

Celiac disease is separated from the authors' NCGS reality, no absolute safety claim is made, cross-contamination (fryer, grill plate, tongs, pan) is addressed explicitly, and the FAQ states outright that the phrases change what the kitchen says, not what it does.
Both external sources carry explicit as-of dates (August 2026), the publication date is stated, and reformulation risk is flagged as a standing caveat.
The load-bearing labelling fact is correct and correctly attributed to the 시행규칙 별표 2, the 밀가루/밀 distinction is handled precisely, and 알러지/알레르기, 양조간장/조선간장/혼합간장 are all described accurately.

A dedicated section tells the reader to read 원재료명 in hand, links a scan method, suggests phoning ahead, and links the manufacturer page so the soy-sauce claim can be checked without trusting the author.

findings.quote: Traditional **조선간장 / 한식간장** — the meju-based kind used for soups and namul — carries no wheat
findings.why: This is a category-level compositional claim presented as fact with no source, in a paragraph whose other claim (양조간장 contains wheat) is properly cited to Sempio. A reader could carry it forward as 'the traditional kind is fine' even though the article's own hedge follows.
findings.fix: Cite one primary source for the traditional 한식간장 definition (e.g. the 식품의 기준 및 규격 간장 유형 분류, or a manufacturer ingredient list for a 조선간장 product), or mark the sentence as the authors' understanding rather than a category fact.

findings.quote: We are describing what has worked for us in Seoul and Gyeonggi as a couple managing NCGS.
findings.why: Earlier the article states the experience base is 'across Seoul, Gyeonggi and Cheonan'. The two scope statements disagree, which weakens the reader's ability to judge how far the first-hand claims extend.
findings.fix: Make the two scope statements identical — either include Cheonan in both, or drop it from the earlier one and explain why it is excluded from the summary.
